title: Haseeb Danyal
tagline: A map of how Haseeb Danyal’s public work makes design more legible: for users, business partners, and the designers doing the work.
credit: An independent StoryTellr study by Nikhil Khedkar.
disclaimer: Built from Haseeb Danyal’s public professional work and employer profile, read on 2026-09-30. Project outcomes and colleague comments are attributed to their publishers and have not all been independently verified. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Haseeb Danyal, mobileLIVE, or TribalScale.

How we got buy-in on our design practices with a UX Playbook

nodes.title: Haseeb Danyal
nodes.summary: A product designer and design leader whose public work spans product experiences, design operations, and the growth of design teams.
nodes.evidence: Design Leadership @ TribalScale

nodes.title: Software to product design
nodes.summary: Haseeb’s bio describes a move from software engineering into product design, connecting technical practice with user experience.
nodes.evidence: he decided to switch careers from software engineering to product design

nodes.title: Design maturity
nodes.summary: His bio frames the work as helping organizations build design maturity through team coaching, processes, and frameworks.
nodes.details: The bio describes this as seven years of work but provides no start date; that duration is presented as Haseeb’s own claim.
nodes.evidence: enabling organizations to embrace design centricity and lead design maturity

nodes.title: Design leadership at TribalScale
nodes.summary: TribalScale’s profile places him in its design leadership function and describes work across product design, research, and leadership.
nodes.details: The experience and reach claims on the employer profile are not independently verified here.
nodes.evidence: 15+ years of experience in product design, user research, and design leadership

nodes.title: PATARI redesign
nodes.summary: An older portfolio project shows product and visual-design work predating the later DesignOps case studies.
nodes.evidence: Published June 24th 2017

nodes.title: DesignOps practice
nodes.summary: Across his case studies, DesignOps appears as the connective work around design: organizing files, clarifying processes, and helping people collaborate.
nodes.details: This is a synthesis across the cited projects, rather than a formal job title attached to every initiative.
nodes.evidence: DesignOps is a collective term for addressing challenges such as growing teams and creating efficient workflows

nodes.title: People, process, craft
nodes.summary: NN/g’s framework gives useful context for the portfolio: DesignOps combines team support, workable processes, and consistent design craft.
nodes.evidence: the orchestration and optimization of people, processes, and craft

nodes.title: Repeated handovers
nodes.summary: The mobileLIVE article describes repeated walkthroughs and duplicate presentation work as a drain on designers’ time.
nodes.evidence: repeated walkthroughs and presentation tasks reduced time for solving user and product problems

nodes.title: A shared design language
nodes.summary: The proposed response is to make design files and decisions understandable to people outside the design team.
nodes.evidence: the shared language will help stakeholders understand how design files are organized and documented

nodes.title: Design-file statuses
nodes.summary: A shared set of status labels lets collaborators see whether a screen or flow is underway, ready for review, approved, or archived.
nodes.evidence: the key allows anyone coming into the design file to understand its status

nodes.title: Comment keys
nodes.summary: Comment keys document design decisions, questions, and concerns in the files where the work is discussed.
nodes.evidence: comment keys document design decisions, clarifications, ideas, and concerns

nodes.title: The UX playbook
nodes.summary: An interactive Figma prototype translated the team’s design activities into an explanation business stakeholders could use.
nodes.evidence: the UXD playbook was an interactive Figma prototype

nodes.title: Five stages of design
nodes.summary: The playbook grouped work into Discover, Research, Sketch, Design, and Measure, making the parts around interface production visible too.
nodes.evidence: Discover, Research, Sketch, Design, and Measure

nodes.title: A living team document
nodes.summary: The playbook was described as an evolving document owned by the design team rather than a one-time presentation.
nodes.evidence: a live document that is owned by every designer in our team

nodes.title: Designer career ladder
nodes.summary: At mobileLIVE, Haseeb’s case study describes a career framework intended to make growth paths and expectations clearer as the design team expanded.
nodes.evidence: we started by building a career ladder for all design roles within the organization

nodes.title: Two growth tracks
nodes.summary: After senior level, designers could choose an individual-contributor or leadership track, and the case study says switching remained possible.
nodes.evidence: designers can decide to pursue either the individual contributor path or the leadership path

nodes.title: Clear role expectations
nodes.summary: The framework set expectations for each design role, mixing craft skills with communication and other people skills.
nodes.evidence: a good mix of hard and soft skills

nodes.title: Annual skill assessments
nodes.summary: A yearly assessment compared role expectations with input from designers, client-side stakeholders, and design leads.
nodes.evidence: we run skill assessments once a year

nodes.title: A word-based skill scale
nodes.summary: The example uses plain-language ratings from improving to excelling; the displayed radar chart is hypothetical.
nodes.details: The source says the scale was learned from Salesforce. That provenance is reported by the author and not separately investigated.
nodes.evidence: 0 non-scoring; 1 improving; 2 achieving; 3 excelling

nodes.title: Goals and weekly check-ins
nodes.summary: The article links assessment results to achievable development goals and weekly one-on-ones between designers and leads.
nodes.evidence: the conversation is carried over to weekly one-on-ones

nodes.title: JazzCash home redesign
nodes.summary: Haseeb describes leading the redesign while also working hands-on on selected experiences, bringing team alignment and product UX into one case.
nodes.evidence: I led the redesign for one of the largest and most actively used mobile wallets in South Asia

nodes.title: Research shapes direction
nodes.summary: Interviews with users and business stakeholders informed the pain points and priorities described in the redesign case study.
nodes.evidence: interviews with users and our business stakeholders

nodes.title: Access, discovery, control
nodes.summary: The design goals focused on making actions easier to find, improving service discovery, and giving users more control.
nodes.evidence: improve service discoverability; allow users to have more control over their experience

nodes.title: Personalized home services
nodes.summary: A central section let people place their four most-used services on the home screen; business-promoted services sat separately below it.
nodes.evidence: customize their top four most used services

nodes.title: Reported feature uptake
nodes.summary: The portfolio reports that more than 85% of users used and customized the feature within two months.
nodes.details: This is a project outcome as reported in Haseeb’s portfolio; the underlying analytics or an independent source was not available in the material reviewed.
nodes.evidence: over 85% of users using it and customizing their most used services within the first two months

nodes.title: Design system as work grew
nodes.summary: Reusable components were added alongside new screens, with team huddles used to review and accept additions.
nodes.evidence: we built our design system along the way with every new screen

nodes.title: Usability measures
nodes.summary: The portfolio reports SEQ and SUPR-Q scores for the redesigned experience, as well as a SUS result for account information.
nodes.details: The page describes these results but does not provide sample sizes, test dates, or study materials; read them as portfolio-reported figures.
nodes.evidence: SEQ scores between 6 and 7; SUPR-Q scores of 4 and above

nodes.title: Not a Journal challenge
nodes.summary: A short self-initiated challenge shows another version of the same research-to-interface process, from interviews through personas, journey, prototypes, and reflection.
nodes.evidence: I talked to three friends
nodes.details: Haseeb says the project took roughly 12 hours and notes that a broader interview sample could have surfaced more insights.

nodes.title: Leadership as enablement
nodes.summary: Haseeb’s leadership essay defines the job through creating safety, guidance, and room for people to grow, rather than only assigning work.
nodes.evidence: leadership roles entail a lot of responsibility

nodes.title: Meaningful one-on-ones
nodes.summary: He recommends tailoring check-ins to people’s concerns, motivations, roles, and goals.
nodes.evidence: tailor every new conversation around them, not you

nodes.title: Empower, don’t micromanage
nodes.summary: The essay argues that leaders succeed when their teams can deliver without constant intervention.
nodes.evidence: you succeed when your people can deliver without you stepping in at every turn

nodes.title: Colleagues describe the practice
nodes.summary: Hosted testimonials from a design-operations leader and designers praise Haseeb’s team-building, coaching, and collaborative style.
nodes.details: These are first-person recommendations published on Haseeb’s site. They show how named colleagues describe working with him, not an independently sampled assessment.
nodes.evidence: Mark Lannutti says Haseeb set up a DesignOps practice and standardized design roles, career paths, and work processes

nodes.title: Measure the whole system
nodes.summary: In a 2024 essay, Haseeb groups design-team measurement around who is on the team, how work happens, and the outcomes it creates.
nodes.evidence: who is on the team, how the work gets done, and how the work creates business impact

edges.label: includes reuse as a measure of

stories.title: Making design legible
stories.summary: One strand of the work starts with repeated handovers and ends with a shared language: status labels, documented decisions, and a playbook that gives stakeholders context before the pitch.

stories.title: From process to growth
stories.summary: The career framework turns team operations into individual development: clear roles, two paths after senior level, yearly input, then recurring conversations and goals.

stories.title: Research to interface
stories.summary: The JazzCash case moves from interviews to product goals, a personalized home, and a design system. Adoption and usability results are reported by the portfolio, not independently verified here.

stories.title: Leading through enablement
stories.summary: Haseeb’s published leadership principles emphasize tailored one-on-ones, growth, and autonomy. Colleague testimonials hosted on his site describe related experiences, with the source and perspective kept visible.
